section_summary: This section documents the South Manchuria Railway Company’s financial condition, expanding workforce, traffic revenues, subsidiary enterprises, and proposed five-year investment program. It repeatedly examines the conflict between the company’s commercial and shareholder interests and the Kwantung Army’s determination to subordinate it to military and “national policy,” including plans to relocate offices, divide subsidiaries, and unify railway management under Manchukuo. Other records cover the Kochu Kungssu trading subsidiary, a Peiping–Mukden through-freight agreement, and a detailed but incomplete analysis of the company’s 1935–1936 balance sheet.

subfiles.title: Appointment of Matsuoka and the Future Policy of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.about: Analyzes Yosuke Matsuoka’s appointment as railway president and the conflict between financial restraint and the Kwantung Army’s development program.
subfiles.summary: The concluding portion contrasts Matsuoka’s publicly reported preference for agriculture and sound finance with military demands for industrial expansion in Manchuria and North China. It argues that Count Hayashi was removed because he impeded military control of the railway and warns that Matsuoka’s planned meeting with General Minami could resolve the dispute or produce an open rupture. Grummon also considers whether Matsuoka’s apparent independence was tactical or reflected genuine concessions forced on the Army by Japanese financial interests.

subfiles.title: Revision of Estimate by the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.from: Troy L. Perkins, American Vice Consul
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a drastic reduction in the railway company’s proposed expenditures for new enterprises in fiscal 1936.
subfiles.summary: The company cut its enterprise estimate from 89 million to 31 million yen in retrenchment, deleting Fushun power and shale-oil expansion and other projects, against 70 million spent in 1934.

subfiles.title: Departmental Note on South Manchuria Railway Income
subfiles.about: Summarizes the railway company’s income during the eight months ending November 30, 1935.
subfiles.summary: Note: passenger receipts rose ten percent, freight fell similarly, coal slightly down, overall income down about six percent, with rain-damaged soybeans cutting freight.

subfiles.title: Income of the South Manchuria Railway Company, April 1–November 30, 1935
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Provides detailed passenger and freight revenue figures for the first eight months of the 1935 fiscal year.
subfiles.summary: April 1-November 30, 1935 income fell 5.8 percent to about 81 million yen despite record passenger revenue; freight fell 10.8 percent on less construction shipping and flood-hit soybeans; rolling-stock shortages after regauging former Chinese Eastern lines.

subfiles.title: Departmental Note on Railway Rationalization
subfiles.about: Summarizes tentative plans to rationalize the South Manchuria Railway Company’s subsidiary holdings.
subfiles.summary: Note: the company wished to keep railway-related enterprises like the Anshan steel mills and Manchuria Chemical Industries and sell unrelated holdings such as its oil-refinery share and sugar refinery.

subfiles.title: Tentative Plans for the Rationalization of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports plans to reduce subsidiary spending and sell interests in roughly thirty controlled companies.
subfiles.summary: Subsidiary spending would fall from about 90 million to 36-38 million yen, with thirty of seventy subsidiaries to be sold; Grummon links this to financing Matsuoka's five-year program in Manchuria and North China.

subfiles.title: Formal Organization of the Kochu Kungssu
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the establishment of Kochu Kungssu as a South Manchuria Railway subsidiary for trade and investment in China.
subfiles.summary: Kochu Kungssu was organized at Dairen December 20 with 10 million yen capital, planned 40-50 million, headed by Shinji Sogo with industrial and banking advisers; officials say its North China studies are economic, not political.

subfiles.title: Articles of Association of Kochu Kungssu
subfiles.to: Enclosure to the American Consulate’s December 23 despatch
subfiles.about: Sets out the capital, purposes, governance, accounting, and profit-distribution rules of Kochu Kungssu.
subfiles.summary: Articles of Kochu Kungssu: a Dairen joint-stock company with 10 million yen in 200,000 shares for China trade and financing Chinese enterprises, with governance, accounts, reserves and dividend rules.

subfiles.title: Increase in Number of South Manchuria Railway Company Employees Since the Manchurian Incident
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Examines the rapid growth and changing ethnic composition of the railway company’s workforce after 1931.
subfiles.summary: Permanent employment rose from 32,362 in October 1931 to 52,699 in January 1936, with over 121,000 under company direction; Japanese employment nearly doubled while Chinese stayed static, contradicting Japanese claims; salaries declined.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Telegram 135 on Through Freight Service
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a China telegram concerning a Peiping–Mukden and South Manchuria Railway freight agreement.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: the two railways signed a March 6 agreement for through freight-car service starting May 1.

subfiles.title: Telegram 135 from Peiping on North China Developments
subfiles.about: Reports the through-freight agreement and several Japanese political and military personnel developments in North China.
subfiles.summary: Peiping telegram 135: through freight service between the Peiping-Mukden and South Manchuria railways strengthens Manchukuo-North China links; Japanese advisers to the Hopei-Chahar Council, Matsumuro to replace Doihara; Johnson discounts Isogai's remarks on Sung Che-yuan.

subfiles.title: Reorganization Plans of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Assesses proposals to move the company headquarters to Hsinking and unify railway administration in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Grummon: moving headquarters from Dairen would be delayed by cost and finances, seen as Kwantung Army tightening control; management unification seems decided, turning the company into an instrument of state and military policy.

subfiles.title: Departmental Summary of the Kwantung Army–Railway Company Relationship
subfiles.about: Summarizes Grummon’s June 19 confidential despatch about military plans to reorganize the South Manchuria Railway Company.
subfiles.summary: Summary: proposals to admit Manchukuo capital, place the railway under Manchukuo administration, expand North China activities, separate non-transport businesses, and control it through Kwantung institutions; employees oppose and Matsuoka expects eventual merger with the State Railways.

subfiles.title: Relation of the Kwantung Army to the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes the fundamental conflict between the Kwantung Army and the railway company’s commercial and shareholder interests.
subfiles.summary: Grummon argues that military authorities sought to dismantle or subordinate the company even though its officers and Japanese financial interests resisted. A reported Army plan would reduce it to transportation functions, transfer utilities, newspapers, and other enterprises, and bring it under control from Hsinking. Matsuoka publicly defended the company’s finances and investment program but privately admitted that returns might take ten or twenty years and that further investment was necessary to protect existing commitments. Grummon concludes that the company’s survival as an autonomous entity was seriously threatened.

subfiles.title: Outline of Plan Proposed by the Army for Reorganization of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.from: Kokutsu despatch, Tokyo, published in Manshu Nichi Nichi Shimbun
subfiles.about: Presents the Army’s proposed legal, financial, and administrative restructuring of the railway company.
subfiles.summary: Army plan: a Japanese juridical person running railways and harbors in Manchukuo, North Korea and North China with a one billion yen capital, separating commercial enterprises, consolidating coal, moving utilities and newspapers to Manchukuo, and ending tax exemption.

subfiles.title: Transfer of Offices of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports company and municipal opposition to moving railway offices from Dairen to Hsinking or Mukden.
subfiles.summary: A company officer calls the Hsinking move a device for Kwantung Army domination; costs of abandoning Dairen housing will likely delay it; Dairen representatives fear economic effects though Mayor Marumo will not block it.

subfiles.title: Departmental Note on Grummon’s South Manchuria Railway Balance-Sheet Report
subfiles.about: Highlights selected findings from Grummon’s detailed analysis of the company’s balance sheet.
subfiles.summary: Note on Grummon's report: record 49.62 million yen profit, assets near two billion yen, a five-year plan needing about 436 million in debentures, investor worry about military interference, 540 million advanced to Manchukuo, and many unprofitable affiliates showing dominance over Manchurian industry.

subfiles.title: Comments on the Balance Sheet of the South Manchuria Railway Company for Fiscal Year 1935–1936
subfiles.to: Erle R. Dickover, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Provides an extensive financial and operational analysis of the railway company’s fiscal 1935–1936 balance sheet.
subfiles.summary: Despite tighter censorship and reduced access to company accountants, Grummon analyzes record profits, nearly two billion yen in assets, capital calls, reserves, bonds, investments, current accounts, deposits, and liabilities. Particular attention is given to Matsuoka’s 436-million-yen five-year debenture program, investor reluctance caused by military pressure, and the company’s large advances to Manchukuo railway construction. The report reviews new railway lines, ports, collieries, shale-oil works, passenger and freight traffic, employee funds, hotels, and local administration, while warning that official accounting often concealed losses imposed by national policy. The document continues beyond page 236.
